--- title: "Structural parallels" --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("analysis/_setup.R") d0 <- as.data.table(dk_mortality)[year == 2000] d1 <- as.data.table(dk_mortality)[year == 2019] m10 <- load_icio(icio_synth[["2010"]]) m20 <- load_icio(icio_synth[["2020"]]) ``` ::: This page covers four claims, each backed by code: 1. The Leontief inverse is the fundamental matrix of an absorbing Markov chain. 2. Multi-factor decompositions are not unique, and both fields fix this the same way: by averaging over all orderings (Shapley). 3. LTRE and Leontief-based attribution are the same operation, sensitivity × change. The two sensitivities even have the same form. 4. The concepts map one-to-one onto each other. ## 1. One matrix inverse behind both fields `leontief_inverse()` and `fundamental_matrix()` call the same internal routine, $M \mapsto (I - M)^{-1}$. It exists when the spectral radius of $M$ is below 1, which is also when the Neumann series $I + M + M^2 + \dots$ converges. Both fields use the column convention. $A_{ij}$ is the input from sector $i$ per unit of output of sector $j$, and $U_{ij}$ is the probability of moving from state $j$ to state $i$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # An absorbing Markov chain: three living states; death is absorbing (column shortfall) U <- matrix(c(0.85, 0.05, 0.00, 0.08, 0.80, 0.05, 0.02, 0.10, 0.85), 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(to = c("healthy", "ill", "disabled"), from = c("healthy", "ill", "disabled"))) # A small input-output system: three sectors A <- matrix(c(0.15, 0.25, 0.05, 0.20, 0.05, 0.40, 0.10, 0.20, 0.10), 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(supplier = c("agri", "manuf", "services"), user = c("agri", "manuf", "services"))) N <- fundamental_matrix(U) B <- leontief_inverse(A) identical(fundamental_matrix(U), leontief_inverse(U)) # literally the same computation ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: {layout-ncol=2} ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Fundamental matrix N: expected years in state i (row), starting from state j (column). The total row is life expectancy by starting state.'} ```{.r .cell-code} round(expected_time_in_state(U), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` healthy ill disabled healthy 8.06 2.42 0.81 ill 4.19 7.26 2.42 disabled 3.87 5.16 8.39 total 16.13 14.84 11.61 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Leontief inverse B: output of sector i (row) needed per unit of final demand for sector j (column). The total row gives the output multipliers.'} ```{.r .cell-code} round(rbind(B, total = colSums(B)), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` agri manuf services agri 1.298 0.394 0.247 manuf 0.369 1.273 0.586 services 0.226 0.327 1.269 total 1.893 1.993 2.102 ``` ::: ::: ::: | | Absorbing Markov chain | Input-output model | |---|---|---| | Matrix | $U$: transitions among transient states | $A$: input coefficients | | Leakage | $1 - \mathbf{1}'U$: death | $1 - \mathbf{1}'A$: value added | | $(I - M)^{-1}$ | $N$: expected visits | $B$: total requirements | | $\mathbf 1'(I-M)^{-1}$ | life expectancy by starting state | output multipliers | | leakage × inverse | $(1 - \mathbf 1'U) N = \mathbf 1'$: everyone dies eventually | $v'B = \mathbf 1'$: all final demand becomes value added | The last row is the identity that makes Leontief decompositions of exports add up. In the chain it says that absorption is certain: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rbind(death_x_N = (1 - colSums(U)) %*% N, va_x_B = (1 - colSums(A)) %*% B) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` healthy ill disabled [1,] 1 1 1 [2,] 1 1 1 ``` ::: ::: An ordinary life table is the special case with one transient state per age and survival probabilities on the subdiagonal. With $a_x = 1/2$, the chain reproduces period life expectancy exactly, as $e_0 = \mathbf 1'N e_1 - \tfrac12$: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lt <- life_table(d1$mx, ax = rep(0.5, nrow(d1))) n <- nrow(lt); Ulx <- matrix(0, n, n) Ulx[cbind(2:n, 1:(n - 1))] <- 1 - lt$qx[-n] c(life_table_e0 = lt$ex[1], markov_e0 = unname(expected_time_in_state(Ulx, start = c(1, rep(0, n - 1)), correction = 0.5)["total"])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` life_table_e0 markov_e0 81.19536 81.19536 ``` ::: ::: ## 2. Shapley on both sides: sequential decompositions depend on the order If an outcome depends on $K$ factors, switching them one at a time from their old to their new values always adds up. The size of each factor's effect, however, depends on the order in which the factors are switched. Das Gupta's standardisation [@dasgupta1993] and the "average of all polar decompositions" in structural decomposition analysis [@dietzenbacher1998] both average over all $K!$ orderings. That average is the Shapley value [@shapley1953; @shorrocks2013], which `shapley_decomp()` computes for any function. **(a) Demography.** The Danish crude death rate is $f(m, c) = \sum_x m_x c_x$, with age-specific rates $m$ and age composition $c$. As a second example we use Das Gupta's four-factor birth rate. **(b) Trade.** The domestic content of country C1's exports is $f(v, A, e) = \sum_{i \in C1} v_i\, [(I-A)^{-1} e^{C1}]_i$, which depends on the value-added coefficients $v$, the technology $A$ and the export vector $e^{C1}$. We split $A$ into domestic and foreign input blocks, which gives four players. Data: the synthetic tables, 2010 → 2020. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # (a) CDR, two players cdr <- function(p) sum(p$m * p$c) x0 <- list(m = d0$mx, c = d0$pop / sum(d0$pop)); x1 <- list(m = d1$mx, c = d1$pop / sum(d1$pop)) # (a') Das Gupta Example 2.3, four players dg <- function(p) p$birth_preg * p$preg_actw * p$actw_prop * p$w_prop f71 <- list(birth_preg = 25.3, preg_actw = 0.214, actw_prop = 0.279, w_prop = 0.949) f79 <- list(birth_preg = 32.7, preg_actw = 0.290, actw_prop = 0.473, w_prop = 0.986) # (b) domestic content of C1's exports, four players c1 <- seq_len(m10$N) dc_c1 <- function(p) { e <- p$e; e[-c1] <- 0; sum((p$v * solve(diag(length(e)) - p$A, e))[c1]) } io <- function(m) list(v = unname(m$Vc), A = unname(m$A), e = unname(m$E)) dom <- outer(rep(m10$k, each = m10$N), rep(m10$k, each = m10$N), "==") grp <- list(v = rep("v (VA coefficients)", m10$GN), A = ifelse(dom, "A domestic", "A foreign"), e = rep("e (exports)", m10$GN)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} s_cdr <- shapley_decomp(cdr, x0, x1) s_dg <- shapley_decomp(dg, f71, f79) s_io <- shapley_decomp(dc_c1, io(m10), io(m20), groups = grp) check <- function(s, label) data.table(case = label, players = length(s), f_change = attr(s, "f2") - attr(s, "f1"), sum_shapley = sum(s), gap = sum(s) - (attr(s, "f2") - attr(s, "f1"))) rbind(check(s_cdr, "Danish CDR"), check(s_dg, "Das Gupta birth rate"), check(s_io, "C1 domestic content")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|case | players| f_change| sum_shapley| gap| |:--------------------|-------:|----------:|-----------:|---:| |Danish CDR | 2| -0.0015796| -0.0015796| 0| |Das Gupta birth rate | 4| 2.9891394| 2.9891394| 0| |C1 domestic content | 4| 66.9672760| 66.9672760| 0|
::: ::: **Order independence.** Listing the players in a different order gives identical Shapley values: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rev_grp <- grp[c("e", "A", "v")] s_io_rev <- shapley_decomp(dc_c1, io(m10)[c("e", "A", "v")], io(m20)[c("e", "A", "v")], groups = rev_grp) all.equal(as.vector(s_io[names(s_io_rev)]), as.vector(s_io_rev)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: **Sequential decompositions do depend on the order.** `all_orderings()` lists each player's effect under every ordering: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ao <- rbind( all_orderings(cdr, x0, x1)[, case := "(a) Danish crude death rate, per 1000"][ , `:=`(effect = 1000 * effect, shapley = 1000 * shapley)], all_orderings(dg, f71, f79)[, case := "(a') Das Gupta birth rate"], all_orderings(dc_c1, io(m10), io(m20), groups = grp)[, case := "(b) Domestic content of C1 exports"]) ao[, case := factor(case, levels = unique(case))] spread <- ao[, .(orderings = .N, min = min(effect), max = max(effect), shapley = shapley[1]), by = .(case, player)] spread[, lapply(.SD, function(x) if (is.numeric(x)) round(x, 4) else x)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|case |player | orderings| min| max| shapley| |:-------------------------------------|:-------------------|---------:|--------:|-------:|--------:| |(a) Danish crude death rate, per 1000 |m | 2| -4.0187| -3.2952| -3.6569| |(a) Danish crude death rate, per 1000 |c | 2| 1.7156| 2.4391| 2.0774| |(a') Das Gupta birth rate |birth_preg | 24| 0.4193| 1.0008| 0.6889| |(a') Das Gupta birth rate |preg_actw | 24| 0.5091| 1.1590| 0.8125| |(a') Das Gupta birth rate |actw_prop | 24| 0.9968| 1.8139| 1.3829| |(a') Das Gupta birth rate |w_prop | 24| 0.0559| 0.1660| 0.1048| |(b) Domestic content of C1 exports |v (VA coefficients) | 24| -17.6939| -8.6057| -12.9331| |(b) Domestic content of C1 exports |A domestic | 24| -11.0175| -4.8112| -7.6616| |(b) Domestic content of C1 exports |A foreign | 24| 2.6921| 6.6299| 4.4038| |(b) Domestic content of C1 exports |e (exports) | 24| 75.8048| 91.1503| 83.1582|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(ao, aes(x = effect, y = player)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.4) + geom_point(colour = ink2, alpha = 0.45, size = 2.2) + geom_point(data = spread, aes(x = shapley), colour = pal[1], shape = 18, size = 4.5) + facet_wrap(~case, ncol = 1, scales = "free") + labs(x = "Effect of switching the player from old to new values", y = NULL, title = "Sequential effects depend on the ordering; Shapley values do not", subtitle = "Grey: one point per ordering. Blue: Shapley value (mean over all orderings)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Each player's sequential-substitution effect under every ordering (grey points), and its Shapley value, the mean over orderings (blue diamond). The spread of the grey points shows how much a one-ordering decomposition depends on an arbitrary choice.](03-structural-parallels_files/figure-html/fig-orderings-1.png){#fig-orderings width=768} ::: ::: With two players, the Shapley value is exactly Kitagawa's midpoint formula: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} k <- kitagawa2(d0$mx, d1$mx, d0$pop, d1$pop) c(shapley_rate = 1000 * unname(s_cdr["m"]), kitagawa_rate = 1000 * sum(k$rate), shapley_comp = 1000 * unname(s_cdr["c"]), kitagawa_comp = 1000 * sum(k$composition)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` shapley_rate kitagawa_rate shapley_comp kitagawa_comp -3.656938 -3.656938 2.077384 2.077384 ``` ::: ::: ## 3. Sensitivity × change: LTRE and Leontief attribution Both fields also have a first-order alternative to Shapley: weight each entry's change by the derivative of the outcome, evaluated at the midpoint. In demography this is the LTRE [@caswell1989]. In input-output analysis it is the differential form of structural decomposition analysis. The two sensitivities are both outer products: $$ \frac{\partial \lambda}{\partial a_{ij}} = \frac{v_i\, w_j}{\langle v, w\rangle} \qquad\qquad \frac{\partial\, v'(I-A)^{-1}e}{\partial a_{ij}} = (v'B)_i\, (Be)_j . $$ The reproductive value $v$ (what one individual in stage $i$ is worth to future growth) corresponds to the value-added multiplier $v'B$. The stable stage structure $w$ (how much of the population passes through stage $j$) corresponds to gross output $Be$. We compare the first-order attribution with the exact Shapley attribution over the same groups of entries. For the *Hudsonia* projection matrices (1985 → 1988), the groups are fecundity, stasis, growth and retrogression. For the ICIO tables (2010 → 2020, $A$ only, $v$ and $e$ held at 2010), the groups are the input blocks by supplying country. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} h <- local({ e <- new.env(); utils::data("hudsonia", package = "popbio", envir = e); e$hudsonia }) L85 <- unname(h$A85); L88 <- unname(h$A88); ns <- nrow(L85) ij <- expand.grid(i = seq_len(ns), j = seq_len(ns)) type <- matrix(with(ij, ifelse(i == 1 & j > 1, "fecundity", ifelse(i == j, "stasis", ifelse(i > j, "growth", "retrogression")))), ns) lam <- function(M) max(Re(eigen(M, only.values = TRUE)$values)) C_lam <- ltre_fixed(L85, L88) sh_lam <- shapley_decomp(lam, L85, L88, groups = type) # v and e held at 2010; only C1's value added and C1's exports enter (masked vectors) v10 <- unname(m10$Vc); v10[-c1] <- 0 e10 <- unname(m10$E); e10[-c1] <- 0 dc_A <- function(M) sum(v10 * solve(diag(nrow(M)) - M, e10)) supplier <- matrix(paste("inputs from", rep(m10$k, each = m10$N)), m10$GN, m10$GN) C_io <- ltre_fixed(unname(m10$A), unname(m20$A), stat = dc_A, sensitivity = function(M) leontief_sensitivity(M, v10, e10)) sh_io <- shapley_decomp(dc_A, unname(m10$A), unname(m20$A), groups = supplier) cmp <- rbind( data.table(case = "Population growth rate λ (Hudsonia)", group = names(sh_lam), first_order = tapply(as.vector(C_lam), as.vector(type), sum)[names(sh_lam)], shapley = as.vector(sh_lam)), data.table(case = "Domestic content of C1 exports (A only)", group = names(sh_io), first_order = tapply(as.vector(C_io), as.vector(supplier), sum)[names(sh_io)], shapley = as.vector(sh_io))) cmp[, difference := first_order - shapley] cmp[, lapply(.SD, function(x) if (is.numeric(x)) signif(x, 4) else x)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|case |group | first_order| shapley| difference| |:---------------------------------------|:--------------|-----------:|----------:|----------:| |Population growth rate λ (Hudsonia) |stasis | 0.1037000| 0.1083000| -0.0046210| |Population growth rate λ (Hudsonia) |growth | 0.1264000| 0.1114000| 0.0150500| |Population growth rate λ (Hudsonia) |fecundity | 0.0001875| 0.0002503| -0.0000628| |Population growth rate λ (Hudsonia) |retrogression | -0.1701000| -0.1610000| -0.0090890| |Domestic content of C1 exports (A only) |inputs from C1 | -3.8600000| -3.8620000| 0.0028760| |Domestic content of C1 exports (A only) |inputs from C2 | 0.7937000| 0.7901000| 0.0036130| |Domestic content of C1 exports (A only) |inputs from C3 | 0.7444000| 0.7414000| 0.0029560|

|case | exact_change| sum_first_order| first_order_error| relative_error_pct| |:---------------------------------------|------------:|---------------:|-----------------:|------------------:| |Population growth rate λ (Hudsonia) | 0.0589761| 0.0602493| 0.0012732| 2.158875| |Domestic content of C1 exports (A only) | -2.3309451| -2.3215000| 0.0094451| -0.405206|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp[, case := factor(case, levels = unique(case))] cl <- melt(cmp, id.vars = c("case", "group"), measure.vars = c("first_order", "shapley"), variable.name = "method") cl[, method := factor(method, c("first_order", "shapley"), c("First order (LTRE / SDA)", "Shapley (exact)"))] ggplot(cl, aes(x = value, y = group, fill = method)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.4) + geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) + facet_wrap(~case, ncol = 1, scales = "free") + scale_fill_manual(values = pal[1:2]) + labs(x = "Contribution to the change", y = NULL, title = "Two attributions of a change in a matrix-model output", subtitle = "Population projection matrix (top) and input-output technology (bottom)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![First-order (sensitivity × change) and exact Shapley attributions over the same groups of matrix entries. They agree closely for the input-output technology change (first-order total off by 0.4%). For Hudsonia, whose vital rates change a lot between 1985 and 1988, they agree less well: group attributions differ by up to about 14% and the total misses by about 2%. The Shapley values always add up exactly.](03-structural-parallels_files/figure-html/fig-sens-1.png){#fig-sens width=768} ::: ::: ## 4. Mapping table ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Concept map between GVC / input-output decompositions and demographic decompositions, with the ddec function that implements each concept.'} ```{.r .cell-code} data.table( `Input-output / GVC` = c( "Input coefficient matrix A", "Leontief inverse B = (I − A)⁻¹", "Value added v = 1 − 1'A", "Output multipliers 1'B", "v'B = 1' (exports fully allocated to VA origins)", "Technology vs final-demand-structure effects (SDA)", "Polar / sequential decompositions", "Average of all n! polar decompositions", "Differential SDA: ∂f/∂A × ΔA", "∂(v'Be)/∂A = (v'B)'(Be)'", "Double counting in gross exports", "Domestic content of exports"), `Demography` = c( "Transient transition matrix U", "Fundamental matrix N = (I − U)⁻¹", "Death (absorption) 1 − 1'U", "Life expectancy by starting state 1'N", "(1 − 1'U)N = 1' (everyone dies)", "Rate vs composition effects (Kitagawa)", "Stepwise replacement", "Das Gupta standardisation", "LTRE: ∂λ/∂A × ΔA", "∂λ/∂A = v w' / ⟨v, w⟩", "(no analogue: a person is counted once)", "Years lived in a state"), `ddec` = c( "load_icio()$A", "leontief_inverse() = fundamental_matrix()", "value_added_multipliers()", "expected_time_in_state()", "value_added_multipliers()", "kitagawa2()", "sequential_decomp()", "das_gupta_n() / shapley_decomp()", "ltre_fixed()", "leontief_sensitivity() / lambda_sensitivity()", "bm(), kww(), wwz()", "leontief(), gvc_components()")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Input-output / GVC |Demography |ddec | |:--------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------| |Input coefficient matrix A |Transient transition matrix U |load_icio()$A | |Leontief inverse B = (I − A)⁻¹ |Fundamental matrix N = (I − U)⁻¹ |leontief_inverse() = fundamental_matrix() | |Value added v = 1 − 1'A |Death (absorption) 1 − 1'U |value_added_multipliers() | |Output multipliers 1'B |Life expectancy by starting state 1'N |expected_time_in_state() | |v'B = 1' (exports fully allocated to VA origins) |(1 − 1'U)N = 1' (everyone dies) |value_added_multipliers() | |Technology vs final-demand-structure effects (SDA) |Rate vs composition effects (Kitagawa) |kitagawa2() | |Polar / sequential decompositions |Stepwise replacement |sequential_decomp() | |Average of all n! polar decompositions |Das Gupta standardisation |das_gupta_n() / shapley_decomp() | |Differential SDA: ∂f/∂A × ΔA |LTRE: ∂λ/∂A × ΔA |ltre_fixed() | |∂(v'Be)/∂A = (v'B)'(Be)' |∂λ/∂A = v w' / ⟨v, w⟩ |leontief_sensitivity() / lambda_sensitivity() | |Double counting in gross exports |(no analogue: a person is counted once) |bm(), kww(), wwz() | |Domestic content of exports |Years lived in a state |leontief(), gvc_components() |
::: ::: ## Limits and divergences The parallels are real, but the fields use them for different purposes: * **Tracing vs comparison.** GVC decompositions are *accounting* exercises within a single table. They trace where the value in one flow comes from, through a network, and need no counterfactual. Demographic decompositions (Kitagawa, Das Gupta, Arriaga, LTRE) compare *two* states and attribute the difference to factors, which is inherently counterfactual. Structural decomposition analysis is the input-output technique that corresponds to them; the KWW, WWZ and BM decompositions are not. * **Double counting has no demographic analogue.** In gross trade flows the same value added can cross borders several times, and most of the work in KWW, WWZ and BM is deciding where to record it (source vs sink, exporter vs world perspective). A person-year in a life table is counted once. * **Linearity.** The Leontief model is linear in final demand, so attribution to final demand is exact and unique. Non-uniqueness only appears when $A$ or $v$ also change. Life expectancy and $\lambda$ are nonlinear in the rates, so every demographic decomposition needs an approximation (first order, Arriaga's sequential split) or an averaging rule (Shapley, Horiuchi's continuous path [@horiuchi2008]). * **Arriaga is sequential.** Its age contributions depend on the direction of comparison. It is exact in total but not symmetric, unlike Shapley or the symmetrised Arriaga variants in `LEdecomp`. * **Cost.** Exact Shapley needs $2^K$ evaluations, which is cheap for a few factors or groups but impossible for every cell of a large ICIO table. That is why first-order (LTRE / differential SDA) attributions remain useful in practice. The comparison above shows they are accurate when changes are moderate. * **Kitagawa and Oaxaca-Blinder.** The Kitagawa decomposition is also linked to the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition of mean differences in economics [@oaxaca2025], which is a third member of the same family.
